author: Cyril of Alexandria
occasion: Brief exegetical comments on Psalm verses, explaining how the resurrection of sinners differs from that of the righteous and how Psalm 2:7 reveals the eternal and incarnate Sonship of Christ.
argument: On Psalm 1:5, Cyril argues that sinners will rise again but will not share the rank, honor, and reward of the righteous, since their lot is distinct. On Psalm 2:7, he explains that the Son is eternally begotten from the Father's essence, and that 'today I have begotten you' refers to his birth in the flesh from the Virgin. He insists that the incarnate Word remains the Father's own Son by nature, and that this faith is the faith in which Christians are baptized.

outline.move: Explains that sinners may receive mercy but will not be numbered among the righteous, whose reward is eternal.
Introduces Psalm 2:7 and states that the eternal Son and Word became flesh and underwent human birth while remaining the Father's own Son.
Distinguishes the eternal 'you are' from the temporal 'today I have begotten you,' and defends the title Theotokos for the Virgin.
Confesses this as baptismal faith and argues that the incarnate Son did not cease to be Son by nature.

scripture: The author cites Psalms according to the Septuagint numbering. Psalm 1:5 and Psalm 2:7 are cited as in the LXX; modern citations should use the same Psalm numbers. The source also quotes an eschatological blessing, 'Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world,' which is likely Matthew 25:34, but the source does not name the book.
uncertain: The exact date of composition within Cyril's lifetime.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The Virgin ... who gave birth to the incarnate Word and is called Theotokos
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source states she is 'called Theotokos' (ὠνόμασται), but does not explicitly state she 'gave birth to the incarnate Word'—rather, it says she gave birth to 'the Word himself' who 'put on human poverty' (αὐτὸν δὲ μᾶλλον τὸν ἐκ Θεοῦ Πατρὸς Λόγον τὴν ἀνθρώπειαν ὑποδύντα πτωχείαν), with emphasis on the Word becoming human, not that she gave birth to the Word as such.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Christ (quoted Scripture) ... Introduced by 'Χριστοῦ λέγοντος αὐτοῖς'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Χριστοῦ λέγοντος αὐτοῖς· ∆εῦτε οἱ εὐλογημένοι τοῦ Πατρός μου
_unresolved_facts.fix: Christ speaking eschatological blessing (likely Matt 25:34), not quoted Scripture per se—this is a dominical saying, not a Psalm citation.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The Father (quoted Scripture) ... Introduced by 'Κύριος εἶπε πρός με'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Κύριος εἶπεν πρός με Υἱός μου εἶ σύ, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Father is introduced by 'Κύριος εἶπεν πρός με' (with ν), not 'Κύριος εἶπε πρός με' (without ν); and this is the Psalmist speaking, with the Father addressing the Son, not the Father speaking directly in the fragment's frame.
The name/title 'Theotokos' appears in the source and should be listed in names.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The source also quotes an eschatological blessing, 'Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world,' which is likely Matthew 25:34, but the source does not name the book.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Χριστοῦ λέγοντος αὐτοῖς· ∆εῦτε οἱ εὐλογημένοι τοῦ Πατρός μου· κληρονομήσατε τὴν ἡτοιμασμένην ὑμῖν βασιλείαν ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source explicitly attributes this to Christ speaking (Χριστοῦ λέγοντος), not merely quotes it as an unnamed scripture; the brief should note this is presented as Christ's own words, not an anonymous citation.
